title: The Russian Revolution: Causes, Events, Consequences
description: How the 300-year-old Romanov monarchy collapsed in 1917 — the problems of Tsarist Russia, the failed revolution of 1905, the impact of the First World War, the February and October revolutions, the civil war, and the creation of the USSR.

notes.heading: Tsarist Russia and Its Problems
notes.body: In 1900 Russia was a vast empire ruled by **Tsar Nicholas II**, an **autocrat** whose Romanov dynasty had held absolute power for nearly 300 years. There was no elected parliament with real authority, no free press, and a feared secret police, the **Okhrana**, hunted down critics. Society was deeply unequal: the Tsar, aristocrats and the Orthodox Church owned much of the land and wealth, while about 80% of Russians were **peasants** — poor farmers, many of them freed from serfdom only in 1861, who often rented tiny plots and lived close to starvation. In the new industrial cities such as St Petersburg and Moscow, workers endured long hours, low wages and crowded, filthy housing, and trade unions were banned. The empire also ruled many non-Russian peoples — Poles, Finns, Ukrainians and others — who resented forced 'Russification'. Revolutionary ideas were spreading: liberals wanted a constitutional monarchy, while **Marxists** argued that the workers would one day overthrow the whole system. The Tsarist regime looked strong, but beneath the surface it was cracking.

notes.heading: The 1905 Revolution: A Dress Rehearsal
notes.body: Russia's problems exploded in **1905**. The empire had just been humiliated by defeat in the **Russo-Japanese War** (1904–05), which exposed official corruption and incompetence. On **Sunday 22 January 1905**, a peaceful crowd of workers, led by the priest Father Gapon, marched to the Winter Palace in St Petersburg to hand the Tsar a petition asking for reforms. Troops opened fire, killing or wounding hundreds in what became known as '**Bloody Sunday**'. The massacre destroyed the peasant belief in the Tsar as their caring 'Little Father', and protest spread across the empire: strikes paralysed the railways, sailors mutinied on the battleship *Potemkin*, peasants seized land, and a **soviet** (workers' council) was formed in St Petersburg. To save his throne, Nicholas issued the **October Manifesto**, promising an elected parliament — the **Duma** — and civil rights. The concessions divided the opposition, and the regime survived; but the Tsar soon clawed power back, and the Duma was left nearly powerless. Many later called 1905 the 'dress rehearsal' for 1917.

notes.heading: The Impact of the First World War
notes.body: Russia entered the First World War in August 1914 to a wave of patriotic enthusiasm, but the war destroyed the monarchy. The army was huge yet badly led and poorly equipped: soldiers sometimes lacked rifles, boots and shells, and by 1917 around 1.7 million Russian soldiers had been killed. Defeats such as **Tannenberg** (1914) shattered morale, and millions deserted. In 1915 the Tsar fatally took **personal command of the army**, making himself directly responsible for every defeat. He left the government in the hands of the unpopular Tsarina Alexandra and her adviser **Rasputin**, a self-styled 'holy man' whose influence over the royal family (he seemed able to ease their son's haemophilia) scandalised Russia; nobles murdered him in December 1916. On the home front, the war economy broke down: trains carried soldiers instead of food, prices soared, and by early 1917 Petrograd (as St Petersburg was renamed) faced bread shortages and fuel cuts in a bitter winter. Strikes and food riots spread. War had turned discontent into desperation — the regime had lost the support of soldiers, workers and even its own generals.

notes.heading: The February 1917 Revolution
notes.body: In late **February 1917** (March by the modern calendar), events in Petrograd moved faster than anyone expected. On International Women's Day, **23 February**, women textile workers marched demanding bread; within days a quarter of a million people were on strike. The Tsar ordered troops to restore order, and some did fire on crowds — but on **27 February** the Petrograd garrison **mutinied**: soldiers refused to shoot and joined the protesters, handing them rifles. With the capital lost and his generals refusing to help, **Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March 1917**, ending 300 years of Romanov rule. Power was contested by two bodies: the **Provisional Government**, formed by Duma politicians and led from July by the moderate socialist **Alexander Kerensky**, and the **Petrograd Soviet** of workers' and soldiers' deputies. This rivalry was called '**dual power**'. The Provisional Government made a fatal choice: it **continued the war**, kept postponing land reform, and left the old problems unsolved. Popular support drained away towards those who promised immediate change.

notes.heading: Lenin and the Bolsheviks
notes.body: The **Bolsheviks** were a small, disciplined revolutionary party led by **Vladimir Lenin**, a committed Marxist who had spent years in exile. In **April 1917** Germany smuggled Lenin back to Russia in a sealed train, hoping he would stir up trouble and knock Russia out of the war — which he soon did. Lenin's **April Theses** rejected all cooperation with the Provisional Government and promised '**Peace, Land and Bread**' and '**All Power to the Soviets**' — simple slogans that spoke directly to soldiers tired of fighting, peasants hungry for land and workers short of food. Bolshevik membership soared from around 24,000 in February to over 300,000 by October. A failed premature uprising in July forced Lenin to flee to Finland, but the **Kornilov Affair** in August — an attempted military coup by General Kornilov — rescued the party: Kerensky armed the Bolshevik **Red Guards** to defend Petrograd, making them look like the city's saviours. By September the Bolsheviks had majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow soviets, and Lenin judged that the moment for revolution had come.

notes.heading: The October 1917 Revolution
notes.body: Lenin returned secretly to Petrograd and persuaded the Bolshevik leadership to seize power. **Leon Trotsky**, as head of the Petrograd Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee, organised the takeover with remarkable efficiency. On the night of **24–25 October 1917** (6–7 November by the modern calendar), Red Guards and sympathetic soldiers occupied railway stations, bridges, telephone exchanges and government offices almost without a fight. That evening they surrounded the **Winter Palace**, where the Provisional Government sat; a blank shell from the cruiser *Aurora* signalled the attack, and the palace was taken with barely any resistance. Kerensky fled; the government was arrested. The next day Lenin announced a new Soviet government. The first decrees made the Bolsheviks' promises real: the **Decree on Peace** sought an end to the war, the **Decree on Land** gave the nobles' estates to the peasants, and workers were given control of factories. The October Revolution was not a mass uprising but a swift, well-planned seizure of key points — yet it changed world history, putting the first avowedly communist government in power.

notes.heading: Civil War, Communism and the Creation of the USSR
notes.body: The Bolsheviks had to fight to keep power. Lenin ended the war by the harsh **Treaty of Brest-Litovsk** (March 1918), surrendering huge territories to Germany, and shut down the newly elected Constituent Assembly after the Bolsheviks lost the vote. From **1918 to 1921** a savage **civil war** raged between the Bolshevik **Reds** and the anti-Bolshevik '**Whites**' — a loose mix of monarchists, liberals and moderate socialists, backed at times by Britain, France, the USA and Japan. Trotsky built the **Red Army** into a disciplined force, while the Bolsheviks held the central industrial regions and the railways; the divided, scattered Whites never united. Both sides used terror, and the Bolsheviks' secret police, the **Cheka**, executed thousands — including Tsar Nicholas II and his family in July 1918. Under '**War Communism**' the state seized grain from peasants and took over industry, contributing to a famine that killed millions. Victory left the Bolsheviks — now called **Communists** — ruling a ruined country. In **1922** they founded the **Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR)**, the world's first communist state, which lasted until 1991 and reshaped the twentieth century.

flashcards.definition: The last emperor of Russia (reigned 1894–1917), an autocrat who resisted reform. He abdicated in March 1917 and was executed with his family in 1918.
flashcards.example: His decision to take personal command of the army in 1915 made him directly responsible for Russia's military disasters.

flashcards.definition: A system of government in which one person holds absolute power, with no elected parliament able to challenge them.
flashcards.example: Under the Tsar's autocracy there was no free press, and the Okhrana secret police arrested critics of the regime.

flashcards.definition: The massacre of 22 January 1905, when troops fired on a peaceful workers' march to the Winter Palace in St Petersburg, triggering the 1905 revolution.
flashcards.example: The marchers, led by Father Gapon, only wanted to hand the Tsar a petition — hundreds were killed or wounded.

flashcards.definition: The elected parliament promised by the Tsar in the October Manifesto of 1905 to calm the revolution; in practice it was given little real power.
flashcards.example: The Tsar repeatedly changed the voting rules and dissolved Dumas that criticised him.

flashcards.definition: A self-styled 'holy man' whose influence over Tsarina Alexandra — through his apparent ability to ease her son's haemophilia — discredited the monarchy during WWI.
flashcards.example: Alarmed nobles murdered Rasputin in December 1916, but the damage to the Tsar's reputation was done.

flashcards.definition: The temporary government formed by Duma politicians after the Tsar's abdication in February 1917, led from July by Alexander Kerensky.
flashcards.example: Its fatal mistakes were continuing the war and postponing land reform, which drove people towards the Bolsheviks.

flashcards.definition: An elected council of workers' and soldiers' deputies, first formed in 1905 and revived in 1917; the Petrograd Soviet rivalled the Provisional Government.
flashcards.example: 'Dual power' described the rivalry between the Petrograd Soviet and the Provisional Government in 1917.

flashcards.definition: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin, leader of the Bolshevik Party, who returned from exile in April 1917 and led the October Revolution; first head of the Soviet state.
flashcards.example: His slogans 'Peace, Land and Bread' and 'All Power to the Soviets' won the Bolsheviks mass support in 1917.

flashcards.definition: The disciplined Marxist revolutionary party led by Lenin, which seized power in October 1917 and later renamed itself the Communist Party.
flashcards.example: Bolshevik membership grew from about 24,000 in February 1917 to over 300,000 by October.

flashcards.definition: Brilliant Bolshevik organiser: as head of the Petrograd Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee he planned the October takeover, then built and commanded the Red Army in the civil war.
flashcards.example: Trotsky's Red Guards seized Petrograd's bridges, stations and telephone exchanges in a single night in October 1917.

flashcards.definition: The two sides in the Russian Civil War (1918–21): the Bolshevik Red Army versus the anti-Bolshevik Whites, a divided coalition backed by foreign powers.
flashcards.example: The Reds won because they held the industrial centre and railways and were united, while the Whites were scattered and divided.

flashcards.definition: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the world's first communist state, founded in 1922 and dissolved in 1991.
flashcards.example: The USSR created after the revolution became a superpower that shaped world history for most of the twentieth century.

questions.stem: Who ruled Russia as an autocrat until his abdication in 1917?
choices: Vladimir Lenin
Tsar Nicholas II
Alexander Kerensky
Leon Trotsky
questions.explanation: Tsar Nicholas II, the last Romanov emperor, held absolute power until he abdicated in March 1917. Lenin led the Bolsheviks, Kerensky led the Provisional Government, and Trotsky organised the October takeover.

questions.stem: Which of these was NOT a serious problem facing Tsarist Russia around 1900?
choices: Peasant poverty and land hunger
Harsh conditions for industrial workers in the cities
A strong elected parliament that blocked all the Tsar's decisions
Resentment of 'Russification' among the empire's non-Russian peoples
questions.explanation: Tsarist Russia was an autocracy with no real elected parliament at all — that was one of the opposition's main complaints. Peasant poverty, harsh factory conditions and the resentment of non-Russian peoples were all genuine problems.

questions.stem: What happened on 'Bloody Sunday' in January 1905?
choices: The Tsar abdicated and fled abroad
The Bolsheviks stormed the Winter Palace
Troops fired on a peaceful workers' march to the Winter Palace, killing or wounding hundreds
Russia declared war on Japan
questions.explanation: On 22 January 1905 troops shot at marchers who had come to petition the Tsar peacefully. The massacre destroyed faith in the Tsar as the people's 'Little Father' and set off the 1905 revolution.

questions.stem: How did Tsar Nicholas II survive the 1905 revolution?
choices: He issued the October Manifesto, promising a Duma and civil rights, which divided his opponents
He resigned and let the army take over
He granted independence to all non-Russian peoples
He banned all newspapers permanently
questions.explanation: The October Manifesto's promise of an elected Duma split the opposition — moderates were satisfied and stopped protesting, leaving the regime free to crush the remaining radicals. The Tsar then clawed back most of his power.

questions.stem: Why is the 1905 revolution sometimes called the 'dress rehearsal' for 1917?
choices: Because it was staged in a theatre
Because it failed to overthrow the Tsar but rehearsed the strikes, soviets and mass protests that succeeded twelve years later
Because the same events happened on exactly the same dates in 1917
Because it was planned in advance by the Bolsheviks
questions.explanation: In 1905 workers went on strike, formed a soviet and briefly shook the regime, but the Tsar survived. The same forces — war weariness, strikes, soviets — returned in 1917, this time destroying the monarchy, so 1905 looks like a practice run.

questions.stem: Which of these best explains why the First World War was a disaster for the Tsarist regime?
choices: Russia won too easily, so soldiers came home bored
The war was over too quickly to affect Russia
Massive casualties, economic breakdown, food shortages and the Tsar's personal responsibility for defeats destroyed support for the monarchy
The war made peasants richer through higher grain prices
questions.explanation: The war killed around 1.7 million Russian soldiers, wrecked the transport and food-supply systems, and sent prices soaring. By taking personal command in 1915, the Tsar tied his own reputation to the defeats — a fatal error.

questions.stem: Who was Rasputin, and why did he damage the monarchy?
choices: A general who lost the war for Russia
A 'holy man' whose influence over the Tsarina and the royal family scandalised Russia and discredited the Tsar
The leader of the Bolshevik Party
The head of the Provisional Government
questions.explanation: Rasputin's hold over Tsarina Alexandra — he seemed able to ease the heir's haemophilia — led to rumours of corruption at court while the Tsar was at the front. His murder by nobles in 1916 showed how desperate even loyalists had become.

questions.stem: What was the decisive event that forced Nicholas II to abdicate in February–March 1917?
choices: The Bolsheviks seized the Winter Palace
Germany invaded and occupied Petrograd
The Petrograd garrison mutinied — soldiers refused to fire on protesters and joined them instead
The Duma voted to become a republic
questions.explanation: The regime's survival depended on the army's loyalty. When the Petrograd soldiers mutinied on 27 February and handed weapons to the protesters, the Tsar lost all means of enforcing his rule and abdicated days later. The Winter Palace seizure came in October.

questions.stem: What was meant by 'dual power' in Russia during 1917?
choices: The rivalry between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet, which both claimed authority after the Tsar's abdication
The sharing of power between Russia and Germany
The joint rule of the Tsar and the Duma
The alliance between the Reds and the Whites
questions.explanation: After February 1917 the Duma's Provisional Government held formal office, but the Petrograd Soviet of workers' and soldiers' deputies commanded the loyalty of the streets and barracks — two rival centres of power in one city.

questions.stem: Which two mistakes above all destroyed popular support for the Provisional Government?
choices: Ending the war too early and giving away too much land
Continuing the unpopular war and postponing land reform
Banning the Bolshevik Party and arresting Lenin
Refusing to hold any elections until 1920
questions.explanation: By fighting on, the government kept the casualties and shortages coming; by delaying land reform, it disappointed the peasants. The Bolsheviks' promises of 'Peace, Land and Bread' directly answered both failures.

questions.stem: What did Lenin's slogans 'Peace, Land and Bread' promise the Russian people?
choices: An end to the war, land for the peasants, and food for the hungry cities
Victory in the war, bigger armies, and more empire
Peace with the Whites, land for the nobles, and bread rationing
Free trade, foreign investment, and lower taxes
questions.explanation: The slogans summed up exactly what the Provisional Government would not deliver: withdrawal from the war, the nobles' estates for the peasants, and an end to food shortages. Their simplicity won the Bolsheviks mass support.

questions.stem: Why did Germany help Lenin return to Russia in April 1917?
choices: Germany wanted Lenin to advise the Tsar on military tactics
Germany hoped he would stir up revolution and knock Russia out of the war
Lenin had agreed to become a German citizen
Germany wanted to sell weapons to the Bolsheviks
questions.explanation: Germany smuggled Lenin home in a sealed train as a weapon of war: if he destabilised Russia and took it out of the conflict, Germany could move its eastern armies west. Lenin did indeed take Russia out of the war at Brest-Litovsk in 1918.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the October 1917 revolution?
choices: A spontaneous uprising of millions that swept the Bolsheviks to power
A swift, well-planned seizure of key buildings and services in Petrograd by Trotsky's Red Guards, meeting almost no resistance
A long siege of the Winter Palace lasting several weeks
A peaceful vote in the Duma that handed power to Lenin
questions.explanation: The October Revolution was a coup executed with military precision: Red Guards occupied the railway stations, bridges, telephone exchanges and government offices overnight, and the Winter Palace fell with barely a fight.

questions.stem: Why did the Reds win the Russian Civil War (1918–21)?
choices: The Whites had no weapons at all
The Reds controlled the industrial centre and railways and were united under Trotsky's Red Army, while the Whites were divided and scattered
Foreign armies fought on the Red side
The Whites surrendered after a single battle
questions.explanation: The Reds held Moscow, Petrograd and the rail network, so they could move troops and supplies internally, and Trotsky forged a disciplined army. The Whites — monarchists, liberals and socialists who agreed on nothing — fought separately on distant fronts.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the most important long-term consequence of the 1917 revolutions was the creation of the USSR. Which evidence best supports this view?
choices: The USSR, founded in 1922, became a communist superpower that shaped global politics until 1991
The revolution changed Russia's calendar
Petrograd was renamed several times
The Romanov family left Russia quietly
questions.explanation: The revolution created the world's first communist state. As the USSR, it industrialised, helped defeat Nazi Germany, and led the communist bloc through the Cold War — consequences that dominated twentieth-century world history.
